Work in your own git worktree of the Wisp plugins repo (orin-dx/wisp-plugins). First `/usr/bin/git fetch -q origin` then `/usr/bin/git merge --no-edit origin/feat/gate-round-limits` (head 76b5e4d1 or later). Read AGENTS.md and shared/references/architecture/decision-records.md.

## Goal
Condense ADRs 011 to 017 (docs/adr/011-*.md ... 017-*.md) to what a reader two years from now needs to understand why the architecture is shaped this way, and move the transient evidence out. These records were written by agents and run 570 to 750 words with run counts, one-off test dates, lists of files and tests changed, round counts from specific projects, and process narration. The owner has not reviewed them and 015 to 017 are unmerged, so rewriting is allowed here (the rule against rewriting accepted records protects reviewed history).

Target form, about 250 to 350 words each, one paragraph per line, no hard wrapping:
- Title, `**Status:**` and `**Date:**` lines (keep as is, including any `Amends:`/`Supersedes:` lines and status wording other records or the index test depend on).
- **Decision:** the rule, imperative, one short paragraph or a tight list.
- **Why:** only the durable forces and constraints (what about the system makes this the right call). A measurement stays only when the number itself is the constraint; otherwise state the finding in words.
- **Rejected:** each alternative with its "because", one line each.
- **Consequences:** what is now true, what it costs, and the trigger that would justify reversing it (`Revisit when ...`).
- `Enforced by` line only where a test, lint, type or hook enforces it (keep existing ones).
- **Evidence:** one line pointing to where the evidence lives (for example `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, the section name).
Cut: run counts and dates of one-off tests, "live run" narration, lists of files, tests and versions changed, "not yet measured" lists (keep a single Revisit-when), investigation narration, and repeated rationale.

## Preserve
Every decision, every rejected alternative with its because, every guardrail, and the cross-references between records. Do not change what a decision says. Keep docs/adr/README.md rows and their `Do not <X> without a new ADR` guardrails working (the index test in tests/test_reference_integrity.py must pass); edit a row only if its wording depended on removed text.

## Move, do not lose, the evidence
For each ADR, make sure the numbers and findings you cut exist in docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md. Add one section "ADR evidence" there with a short subsection per ADR (011 to 017) holding the measurements, counts and limits removed from the record, grouped and deduplicated against what the log already says. Do not edit other docs/evaluations files.

## Checks
Other tests may read ADR text (for example tests/test_spec_unknowns.py, tests/test_navigator_plan.py, tests/test_agent_structure.py); run `just check` and fix any test that pinned wording you condensed by keeping the pinned fact in the ADR. Judge by exit code.

Working rules: use /usr/bin/git for git; avoid the word git in other command text, heredocs and $(...); write scripts with your file tool under your TMPDIR. Commit locally with `/usr/bin/git add -A` then a separate `/usr/bin/git commit` with dangerouslyDisableSandbox true (GPG signing; approved), message ending with `Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01SGj1qDtVs8manZp9LRpuqm`. Do not push. Report your branch and commit, the word count of each ADR before and after, anything you could not condense without losing a decision, and the checks run.

# Decision Records

Decide whether an architectural choice needs a durable record, and write the record so a later reader with no memory of the discussion does not silently reverse it. A record preserves the reason behind a decision, so nobody accepts it blindly or reverses it blindly.

## Write one only when both gates pass

- **Architectural:** the choice sets a boundary, a model, a direction, or a rule that several changes must respect.
- **Expensive to reverse or not obvious from the code:** a reader who sees only the code would plausibly undo it, or undoing it would be costly.

One decision per record. A choice that fails a gate belongs elsewhere.

| Fact | Home |
| :--- | :--- |
| Architecture, model, direction, decision, rejected alternative | Decision record in `docs/adr/` |
| Rule for every session: command, invariant, style, routing | `AGENTS.md` |
| Required behavior | Spec |
| How the system works today | Docs |
| Why one change was made | Commit message |
| Personal preference or correction for one repository | Agent memory, uncommitted |

Agent memory is unshared and goes stale, so a decision never lives only there.

## Form

Title, status, context, decision, options considered, consequences. Each rejected option carries its "because". Keep a record to one or two pages. Records written before this form may state the alternatives inside the context; leave them as written.

Add an `Enforced by` line only when a test, lint, type, or hook enforces the decision. A decision that a check can enforce should have the check; the record explains why it exists.

Add one line to the `docs/adr/README.md` index in the form `Do not <X> without a new ADR`, for a decision an agent could undo without noticing.

## Prose

Keep the causal "because" and the rejected alternative. Cut narration of the discussion, restated code, and hedging. Write one paragraph per line; do not hard-wrap.

## Status and change

Do not rewrite an accepted record's context, decision, or options; the reasoning at the time is what the record preserves. Update its status and links, and fix errors that do not change its meaning. To change a decision, write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded; the old record stays. Keep the active set small by writing records only for decisions that pass both gates.

## Refutation and disposition

Evidence for a record is the code, spec, or constraint it governs. Before proposing a boundary, read the accepted records for that area. Treat a superseded record as history, not a constraint.

- **Write:** both gates pass and no accepted record covers the choice.
- **Supersede:** the new decision reverses an accepted record; cite it and state what changed.
- **Skip:** the choice is a preference, a routine change, or already obvious from the code; put the reason in the commit message.
- **Coverage gap:** if `docs/adr/` is absent, say so. Absence does not prove that no decision governs the area.

1	# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-10-20
5	
6	## Context
7	
8	Every path through the plugins is gated: recon, a spec that may not contain a TBD, a binding exit gate, a plan, a challenger, then implementation with mutation, review and a second exit gate. That fits a contract many things depend on. It does not fit an idea nobody has seen yet.
9	
10	Two real projects (the Orin DX and Techworx sites, September and October 2026) showed the cost. Eight component specs took 51 gate calls in under an hour, every one failed its first gate, and the retry cap of 3 was not enforced. The specs described behavior well and appearance not at all, so the owner asked for drawings and rewrote the gated specs the next day. On 14 October the owner asked for two phases, exploring quickly first and adding specs and tests once ideas narrow, and the audit machinery was stopped by hand; the landing, Tools and Principles pages then took about 30 minutes. Design ideation ran almost entirely outside the plugins: forks and general-purpose agents spent about 24.8 million subagent tokens, more than all the gates together, and decisions were lost between sessions. The plugin skills were also almost never invoked (7 Skill calls in 812 transcripts), so agents reachable only through skills never ran.
11	
12	The evidence and the measurements are in `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/` (the transcript metrics, the unused-agents investigation and the verification notes). Industry practice points the same way: Vercel's product-design skill routes between a read-only shaping mode and a hardening mode, and Anthropic's own guidance says exploratory work may skip planning.
13	
14	## Decision
15	
16	Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.
17	
18	- **`muse/sketch`** produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and a reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
19	- **`smith/spike`** produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works, with what was verified and what was not.
20	- **`muse/promote`** turns a chosen option or a working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
21	- Exploration modes are **non-binding**: no gate, no spec, no test requirement, open questions allowed. They write only to a scratch directory and to the artifact, mark the artifact `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, and stop before implementing. An exploration artifact is never evidence for a gate.
22	- Divergent generation, producing structurally different options without judging them, is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`), as ADR 003 requires for any new cognitive phase. Judging the options stays with the user.
23	- The modes and their rules live in one reference (`shared/references/architecture/modes.md`), loaded by the three skills. The skill is the entry point; its agents are internal.
24	
25	## Options considered
26	
27	- **Loosen the existing gates.** Rejected because the gates earn their cost on stable contracts: the SiteNav work passed 478 end-to-end tests, and loosening a gate for everyone weakens the cases that need it.
28	- **A light flag on each existing skill.** Rejected because one skill would carry two contracts, and the sessions show the orchestrator skipping skills it finds heavy; a separate, named, light skill is easier to choose and easier to evaluate.

# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Context

Every path through the plugins is gated: recon, a spec that may not contain a TBD, a binding exit gate, a plan, a challenger, then implementation with mutation, review and a second exit gate. That fits a contract many things depend on. It does not fit an idea nobody has seen yet.

Two real projects (the Orin DX and Techworx sites, September and October 2026) showed the cost. Eight component specs took 51 gate calls in under an hour, every one failed its first gate, and the retry cap of 3 was not enforced. The specs described behavior well and appearance not at all, so the owner asked for drawings and rewrote the gated specs the next day. On 14 October the owner asked for two phases, exploring quickly first and adding specs and tests once ideas narrow, and the audit machinery was stopped by hand; the landing, Tools and Principles pages then took about 30 minutes. Design ideation ran almost entirely outside the plugins: forks and general-purpose agents spent about 24.8 million subagent tokens, more than all the gates together, and decisions were lost between sessions. The plugin skills were also almost never invoked (7 Skill calls in 812 transcripts), so agents reachable only through skills never ran.

The evidence and the measurements are in `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/` (the transcript metrics, the unused-agents investigation and the verification notes). Industry practice points the same way: Vercel's product-design skill routes between a read-only shaping mode and a hardening mode, and Anthropic's own guidance says exploratory work may skip planning.

## Decision

Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.

- **`muse/sketch`** produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and a reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
- **`smith/spike`** produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works, with what was verified and what was not.
- **`muse/promote`** turns a chosen option or a working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
- Exploration modes are **non-binding**: no gate, no spec, no test requirement, open questions allowed. They write only to a scratch directory and to the artifact, mark the artifact `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, and stop before implementing. An exploration artifact is never evidence for a gate.
- Divergent generation, producing structurally different options without judging them, is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`), as ADR 003 requires for any new cognitive phase. Judging the options stays with the user.
- The modes and their rules live in one reference (`shared/references/architecture/modes.md`), loaded by the three skills. The skill is the entry point; its agents are internal.

## Options considered

- **Loosen the existing gates.** Rejected because the gates earn their cost on stable contracts: the SiteNav work passed 478 end-to-end tests, and loosening a gate for everyone weakens the cases that need it.
- **A light flag on each existing skill.** Rejected because one skill would carry two contracts, and the sessions show the orchestrator skipping skills it finds heavy; a separate, named, light skill is easier to choose and easier to evaluate.
- **A new plugin for exploration.** Deferred. `muse` is the only plugin that owns UI and design, and `AGENTS.md` lets one plugin hold several skills for heterogeneous intents. The artifact schema is UI-neutral so sketching can move into its own plugin if it is used outside UI work.
- **Leave exploration ad hoc.** Rejected: it produced the largest token cost, the lost decisions and the unreviewed visual defects.

## Consequences

There is now a named, light path for early work, and a stated way back into the gated pipeline. The risks are that an exploration artifact is mistaken for a spec, and that the light path is used where the gated path is needed. The `fidelity` marker, the promote-only rule, the list of cases that must use the full pipeline in `modes.md`, and the required note of which gates were skipped address them. Each new skill and agent needs its Codex counterpart; no plugin version or changelog changes until a release is cut. The new schemas follow ADR 004 and are immutable once published. Whether the light path is chosen when it should be, and whether it speeds exploration without raising the defects found later, is an open evaluation (see `docs/evaluation-methodology.md`).

1	# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
4	**Date:** 2026-10-20
5	
6	## Context
7	
8	Every exit gate returns a `verdict@3` and is told to stop retrying after three attempts and hand the decision to a human. Both rules lived only in prompts. In the two audited projects, 12 of 45 recorded verdicts broke the schema (all 12 by a `verdict_summary` over 300 characters), and eight specs passed their gate with `retry_count` between 4 and 9. The `muse` gate was also told to emit a verdict value that no schema allows. A rule that matters in every run, and can be checked by a program, should not depend on a model remembering it.
9	
10	Claude Code 2.1.271 and later deliver a subagent's report in auto mode through the `SubagentHandback` tool. A `PreToolUse` hook on that tool sees the report in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so the subagent can correct and hand back again. The platform checks were recorded in `docs/verified-facts.md`.
11	
12	## Decision
13	
14	Ship one stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, and register it in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) through `hooks/hooks.json`.
15	
16	- It acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table and lets every other subagent through.
17	- It validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules.
18	- It denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth report passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
19	- It enforces the retry cap in the report: a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with a blocker whose criterion is `escalation_required`.
20	- It fails open: an internal error never blocks a subagent.
21	- `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` appends one line per inspected report, for evaluation.
22	
23	The prompts keep stating the rules, so harnesses without the hook still get the instruction. The hook is the enforcement where the host supports it.
24	
25	## Options considered
26	
27	- **Keep the rules in prompts.** Rejected: the recorded violations show it does not hold.
28	- **Validate in the orchestrator skill.** Rejected: the orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct its own output in place.
29	- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop.** Deferred to WP-603; it can replace the cap check later, but the schema check is useful either way.
30	- **Third-party JSON Schema library.** Rejected: hooks run on user machines with no install step. The validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, and a test covers each.
31	
32	## Consequences
33	
34	Gate conformance is checked on every run in Claude Code auto mode, and the retry cap can no longer be passed silently. 1	# ADR-013: Exit gates list the complete blocker set in round one and cite only known blockers on a retry
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-10
5	
6	## Context
7	
8	In two real projects every spec failed its first gate. Blocker counts per round did not fall: SPEC-001 went 18, 5, 6, 0, 0, 2, 0, 6, 2, 3, 2, 8, 3 across 13 rounds, and eight specs passed only at `retry_count` 4 to 9. The muse gates cost about 8.15 million tokens over 79 calls (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/verification/VERIFY-3.md`, section 5; `CATALOG.md`, WP-50 and WP-212). A zero followed by a nonzero count means a later round found issues an earlier round could have found, or a fix broke something. Each extra round re-reads the whole artifact. ADR 012 already enforces schema conformance and the retry cap by hook, but not round discipline.
9	
10	## Decision
11	
12	- Each exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) states two rules in its `<output>` section, worded the same in all five. In round one (`retry_count` 0 or absent) it lists the complete blocker set. On a retry it cites only blockers from the prior round that remain unresolved, or regressions the fix introduced; any other newly noticed issue is a `coverage_gaps` entry with `blocking: false`.
13	- A blocker names the criterion or section in `criterion`, cites evidence (quoted text or a location) in `finding`, and states the exact change required. A wording-only or style-only issue is a note, never a blocker.
14	- The drafters that feed a spec gate (`muse:drafter`, `scribe:drafter`) load `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` and check their draft against its spec checklist before returning. The checklist and blocker wording live in that one reference.
15	- `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py` additionally denies a blocker or coverage gap whose text field is only whitespace. It checks nothing else about blocker content.
16	
17	Gates stay default-fail and adversarial; no pass condition is relaxed. `verdict@3` is unchanged.
18	
19	## Options considered
20	
21	- **A `verdict@4` with a `regression` or `prior_blocker_id` field on each blocker.** Rejected for now: `verdict@3` already expresses the rule through `blockers` and `coverage_gaps`, and ADR 004 makes a new schema version costly. Revisit if WP-212 needs the hook to tell fix-induced blockers from late-found ones; today the hook cannot, because a retry is a new subagent with no stored prior verdict.
22	- **Hook checks that a blocker has a `location`, a minimum length, or a quote.** Rejected: an `escalation_required` or `missing_mutation_gate` blocker has no location, and a terse correct blocker would be denied. Each denial costs a turn. Only blank text is rejected.
23	- **Make the gate lenient on retries (accept anything not previously listed).** Rejected as stated; the rule does not drop findings, it records them as non-blocking gaps the orchestrator sees.
24	- **Put the rule in the shared constitution.** Rejected: the constitution block is copied byte for byte into every agent (ADR 006), so any change touches all 40 agents; the rule applies only to gates.
25	
26	## Consequences
27	
28	Expected: fewer rounds and fewer tokens per gated spec, with the same defects caught. Not yet measured; a live run (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`) confirms the hook fires and the gates run, not that rounds fall. Costs: a defect a gate misses in round one can now pass as a non-blocking gap on a retry, so the gap list needs a reader; and a gate can only tell a retry from round one if the orchestrator supplies `retry_count` and the prior blockers, which the skills do not yet pass. The skills track must carry the prior blockers into the retry input.
29	
30	**Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (blank text), `tests/test_agent_structure.py` and `tests/test_prompt_alignment.py` (agent shape). The round rules themselves are prompt rules.
31

1	# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-10
5	**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.
6	
7	## Context
8	
9	ADR-009 made the plan's exact implementation code a baseline the implementer may reshape, and kept the plan fully concrete so `challenger` has something to review. The baseline was still required for every task, so `planner` wrote a body for every function, `challenger` policed it, and `implementer` was told not to copy it. The planner prompt was the second-largest agent file.
10	
11	Three observations argue against writing code for every task. Plans of 60 to 130 KB stalled agents in the audited projects (`docs/evaluations/frontend-design/ARCHITECTURE-REVIEW.md`, assumption 10). Anthropic's guidance says instructions written for earlier models are often too prescriptive for current ones and reduce output quality, and its own planner stays at high-level design. And a body the implementer is told it may discard buys little: the guardrail ADR-009 wanted is the plan's scope (files, signatures, tests, criteria), which does not need the body.
12	
13	`plan@1` does not require code. A task requires `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` (an array of strings), and `commit_message`; "exact code" appears only in a field description, and `additionalProperties` is false, so every part of a task other than those fields lives in `steps` strings.
14	
15	## Decision
16	
17	`planner` writes each task as an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`. It adds implementation code only where the logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape would be costly to undo: ordering or concurrency rules, numeric or parsing edge cases, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, algorithms the spec states only by result, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.
18	
19	`challenger` flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified`, and treats a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`. It no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its checks for missing work, ordering, criterion coverage and sibling interfaces are unchanged.
20	
21	No schema change. `plan@1` stays as published (ADR-004). The shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer that reads a plan (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already handles free-text steps.
22	
23	## Options considered
24	
25	- **Keep exact code for every task.** Rejected: it is the cost this record exists to cut, and ADR-009 already made the code non-binding.
26	- **Drop code entirely.** Rejected: a wrong shape in a wire format, a parsing edge or a cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent, and weaker implementers lose a guardrail.
27	- **A plan mode (outcome-level or full-code) chosen per run.** Rejected: it doubles the planner and challenger surface to test, and a per-task rule already covers both ends.
28	- **A `plan@2` with explicit outcome, signature and test fields.** Rejected for now: the existing `steps` array carries the content, and a new version would need every consumer and the pipeline fixtures to move. Revisit if consumers need to read the fields programmatically.
29	- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code.** Rejected: a published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004). The descriptions are stale but harmless.
30	
31	## Consequences
32	
33	Plans are smaller. One run on a six-criterion fixture produced a plan 43% smaller in characters with every criterion still covered (see `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`). Whether implementers do better or worse with outcome-level plans is untested. The risks are that an implementer in a weaker model invents a wrong shape where the plan gave only a signature, and that a plan with no code is harder for `challenger` to falsify. The rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call the planner can get wrong in either direction.
34	
35	ADR-009 stays Accepted as to implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; only its requirement that every task carry the exact code is superseded. Its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.
36	
37	**Enforced by:** `tests/test_navigator_plan.py` checks the planner and challenger rules, the unchanged schema, and that a plan in the new shape validates against `plan@1`.
38

2

1	# ADR-016: Specs state unknowns as assumptions or owner decisions instead of banning them
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-14
5	
6	## Context
7	
8	The spec drafters and exit gates (`scribe`, `muse`) failed a spec for any TBD "regardless of how minor", and the gate-readiness checklist sent every unknown to `non_goals` or `reasoning`. That is a human "definition of ready": everything decided before work starts. In the audited projects every spec failed its first gate, later rounds were mostly wording churn (ADR 015), and the owner rewrote gated specs the day after seeing renders (ADR 011). The ban did not remove unknowns; it moved them where no later stage sees them. `non_goals` reads as an exclusion, so an unknown parked there becomes a silent scope cut, and `reasoning` is never forwarded (ADR 004), so an unknown parked there disappears.
9	
10	What agents need is narrower: every unknown visible, and each one either resolved, stated as an assumption the work proceeds on, or put to the owner when it changes scope, behavior other work depends on, or cost.
11	
12	## Decision
13	
14	- A spec states each unknown in `scope`, one per line after the coverage statement: `Assumption: <the answer the work proceeds on>`, or `Open decision: <question>; options: <A | B>; affects: <criterion ids or scope>`. The convention and the gate disposition live in `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` (Unknowns).
15	- The drafters write unknowns that way and never leave a TBD in a criterion or move an unknown into `non_goals` or `reasoning`. The skills put each open decision to the user before gating and redraft with the answer, which is folded into the spec and the line deleted.
16	- The gates fail an unknown that leaves a criterion untestable, an `Open decision:` line (blocker criterion `owner_decision`, routed to the user rather than the drafter), and an `Assumption:` that actually changes scope, dependent behavior or cost. A stated assumption is not a blocker unless the requirement or code it rests on contradicts it, which is the ordinary claim check of ADR 015.
17	- `spec@1` is unchanged (ADR 004). This replaces the second item of the spec checklist ADR 013 created; the round rules of ADR 013 and the round limit of ADR 015 are unchanged.
18	
19	## Options considered
20	
21	- **Keep the blanket ban.** Rejected: it produced first-round failures and churn without making unknowns go away, and it hid them in fields that mean something else.
22	- **A `spec@2` with `assumptions` and `open_decisions` arrays.** Rejected for now: `spec@1` is named in more than 70 authored files across seven plugins, the Codex skills and the pipeline fixtures, and every consumer already reads `scope`. Revisit when a stage needs to process assumptions programmatically, for example a drift check that re-tests each assumption.
23	- **`non_goals`.** Rejected: it means "excluded", so an unknown there reads as a decision not to build.
24	- **`reasoning`.** Rejected: it is a scratchpad that is never forwarded.
25	- **Criterion text or `rationale`.** Rejected: a criterion states one condition and one observation, `rationale` belongs to `judgment_call` criteria, and a spec-wide assumption has no single criterion.
26	- **`purpose`.** Rejected: it says why the spec exists, not what it covers or rests on.
27	- **Leave open decisions out of the spec and only in conversation.** Rejected: conversation context is compressed and lost; the drafter returns only the spec, so the spec is the one place the skill and the gate both see.
28	
29	## Consequences
30	
31	Fewer first-round failures for unknowns that do not matter, and decisions that do matter reach the user before planning instead of after a render. Planners and implementers read the assumptions in `scope` and can see what the work rests on; an implementer who finds an assumption false reports a `spec_contradiction` on the criteria that depend on it. Costs: the convention is a line prefix in a free-text field, so no schema enforces it, and a drafter can still label a scope change an assumption; the gate's `Assumption:` rule is the guard. Whether rounds and rewrites fall is not yet measured; compare gate rounds per spec before and after with `docs/evaluation-runbook.md`.
32	
33	**Enforced by:** `tests/test_spec_unknowns.py` (a `spec@1` carries both lines without a schema change; the drafters, gates and skills in both harnesses use the convention and no longer ban every TBD) and `tests/test_verification_rules.py` (one owning reference). The gate disposition itself is a prompt rule.
34

1	# ADR-017: Agent bodies drop the `<backstory>` section
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-14
5	**Amends:** ADR-001 and ADR-006, which listed `<backstory>` as a required section. The rest of both records stands: no `<role>` body section, no `success_criteria` checklist, and a byte-identical `<constitution>`.
6	
7	## Context
8	
9	ADR 001 chose an experiential `<backstory>` ("I've seen X...", 2 to 4 sentences) over a role label, on the premise that it shapes judgment where a label would not. The premise was never measured. A backstory is a persona paragraph borrowed from human organizations; it costs tokens in every agent prompt, and it can pull in role behavior. In the 44 agents it mostly restated the failure mode that `<judgment>` already names.
10	
11	A paired ablation tested the premise: 5 runs per condition on seeded defects, with and without the backstory, on `scribe:exit-gate`, `navigator:challenger` and `courier:changeset-analyzer` (Sonnet 5.5), scored on each agent's own output.
12	
13	- **Catch rate:** every seeded defect was found in 5 of 5 runs in both conditions. Gate: an untestable criterion, a criterion contradicting the code, a missing out-of-range case, a fail verdict. Challenger: an uncovered criterion, a wrong task order. Analyzer: a link, a direct-push limit, a bold lead-in, a disposition, a semver impact, a scripting field.
14	- **Size and cost (median per run):** gate 10,346 characters and $0.32 with the backstory, 10,499 and $0.31 without; challenger 6,039 and $0.19, 6,023 and $0.18; analyzer 6,621 and $0.23, 6,359 and $0.23.
15	
16	The limits: the seeded defects were easy, so every run hit the ceiling and the test could not show a backstory helping; three agents of 44, one model, 5 runs each. It shows no measurable effect, not that there is none. Per-run outputs are not reproduced here.
17	
18	## Decision
19	
20	Every agent body defines four sections in order: `<constitution>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, `<output>`, plus the optional `<load_first>` after `<constitution>` as before. All 44 `<backstory>` blocks are removed.
21	
22	A backstory fact the agent needs that appears nowhere else in its `<goal>`, `<judgment>` or `<output>` becomes a plain sentence in `<judgment>`; persona narrative is not kept. One agent needed this: `weaver:intake` now states that `why` names the pain behind the request, not a restatement of the feature. The other 43 backstories restated their agent's goal or judgment.
23	
24	`<role>` and `success_criteria` stay out, and the frontmatter `role:` remains routing metadata. EARS stays confined to `<constitution>` and `<output>` (ADR 002 and ADR 006), now with one fewer interior section.
25	
26	## Options considered
27	
28	- **Keep the backstories.** Rejected: the only measurement shows no difference in what is caught, and they cost tokens in every prompt and may invite role play. Removing them is the cheaper default when nothing supports keeping them.
29	- **Remove them from the three tested agents only.** Rejected: it leaves two structures to author and audit, and the other 41 give no reason to expect a different result.
30	- **Re-run on harder defects first.** Rejected as a precondition: the ceiling effect means a harder run could change the result, but a measured loss is the evidence that should reopen this, and the cost of waiting is the tokens spent in every run meanwhile.
31	
32	## Consequences
33	
34	Each agent prompt is shorter by one paragraph, and the authoring rule has one fewer part. The persona that explained why an agent exists is gone, so a reader of the file sees the failure mode in `<judgment>` but not the incident behind it; the commit history keeps the old text. A real effect on harder tasks, or on other models, would be missed by this evidence.
35	
36	**Restoring one.** If a later measurement shows a loss without the backstory, write a new ADR that supersedes this one, name the agents and the measured difference, and restore the section only for those agents. A restored `<backstory>` sits between `<constitution>` (and `<load_first>`) and `<goal>`; update `PARTS` in `tests/test_agent_structure.py`, the structure rule in `shared/constitution.md`, and the structure statements in `shared/agent-best-practices.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `AGENTS.md` and the mason agents. A useful measurement uses seeded defects hard enough not to saturate, more agents and models, and more than five runs per condition, as in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md`.
37	
38	**Enforced by:** `tests/test_agent_structure.py` (four parts in order, no `<backstory>` or `<role>` section, byte-identical constitution).
39

1	# Wave 0 implementation log
2	
3	Status as of 2026-10-20 on branch `worktree-frontend-design-evaluation`. Five of the Wave 0 work packages in `CATALOG.md` are started or done. Nothing is released: no plugin version, changelog or tag changed (see "Release bookkeeping").
4	
5	| WP | Status | What changed | Verified by |
6	| :-- | :-- | :-- | :-- |
7	| WP-617 Codex model ids | Done | `harnesses/codex/agent-roles/README.md` names `gpt-6-luna`, `gpt-6.1-sol` and `gpt-6-astra` (the selectable models on the Codex models page, 2026-10-20), notes that effort labels are relative and the tiers are unevaluated; generated `dist/codex` copies regenerated | `just marketplace-check`; no `gpt-5.6` or `terra` left in `dist`, `harnesses` or `.agents` |
8	| WP-620 Claude manifests | Done | `tools/sync-claude-manifests.py` generates `plugins/<id>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json` (name, version, description, author) from each `plugin.json`, with `--check`; `just claude-manifests` is in `just check` and CI; `just claude-validate` runs `claude plugin validate --strict` on every plugin and the marketplace | `just claude-validate`: 10 plugins and the marketplace pass `--strict`, and validation now reads each manifest (before, the directory form checked nothing) |
9	| WP-622 AGY and root marketplace | Partly done | Removed the dead `$schema` URL (404) from the root `marketplace.json`; nothing in tests, scripts or CI read it | `just check` |
10	| WP-624 Hook validator spike | Done, registered | `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, a `PreToolUse` hook on `SubagentHandback` that checks exit-gate handbacks against their verdict schema, denies with the errors, caps denials at 3 per agent, enforces the retry cap in the report, and fails open; registered by `hooks/hooks.json` in muse, scribe, smith, sentinel and ranger (ADR 012) | `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (13 tests) and a live run and `verification/scripts/handback-conformance.py` over 45 recorded verdicts |
11	| WP-01 and WP-02 `muse` fixes | Done | The `muse` docs no longer point to a ranger accessibility taxonomy that does not exist (`plugin.json`, README, `SKILL.md`, root `marketplace.json`); the `muse` exit-gate produces `verdict@3` (agent, skill, README, `plugin.json`, Codex skill and catalog, root README table); `verdict@1` has no producer and is kept unchanged | `just check` (66 tests); `just marketplace-check`; validator tests for `muse` routing and for escalation as a blocker |
12	| WP-625 Reasoning-wording lint | Done | `tests/test_reasoning_wording.py` fails on text that demands reproduced reasoning (verbatim, step-by-step, chain of thought), with one documented exception for the immutable `requirement@1` schema | Passes; fails when the probe's demand is planted in an agent file |
13	
14	## What the work found
15	
16	- **`claude plugin validate plugins/<id>` was a false pass** because the manifests sit at the plugin root. With the generated `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` it validates the manifest, and the repo-only keys (`id`, `consumes`, `produces`) stay in `plugin.json` where Claude Code ignores them.
17	- **Recorded gate verdicts nearly all conform to their schemas.** 33 of 45 conform; all 12 violations are `verdict_summary` over 300 characters (`VERIFY-3.md` section 5). A hook would have asked for one trim on about 27% of handbacks.
18	- **`muse` gates mostly emitted `verdict@3`-shaped output** (26 of 36; the other 9 of the 45 files are `scribe` gates) while `muse` documented `verdict@1`, and its prompt told the agent to set `verdict` to `"escalate"`, which no schema allows. WP-02 (done) moved `muse` to `verdict@3` and made escalation an `escalation_required` blocker, as in the other four gates; the validator now checks `muse` against `verdict@3` only.
19	- **A bug in the validator was found only by real data:** a schema property with a list of types (`["string", "null"]`). It is fixed and has a regression test.
20	- **The `requirement@1` schema describes `reasoning` as "chain-of-thought during capture".** It is immutable (ADR 004), agents reach it through a file read and not a prompt, so the lint carries a documented exception; a future `requirement@2` should use the "private scratchpad" wording.
21	
22	## Open items from this work
23	
24	- The README documents AGY installs through the community `agy-plugins-cli`. Fetched source snippets suggest that tool discovers plugins as top-level repository directories, which would not find plugins under `plugins/`. This is unverified; test an install in an isolated environment before changing the README (WP-622, WP-621).
25	- The installed plugins use `shared -> ../../shared` symlinks and the Claude marketplace installs from the `plugins/<id>` subdirectory (`git-subdir`). Whether the symlink resolves after install is untested (WP-621).
26	- The hook is a spike: it needs a plugin `hooks/hooks.json` registration, a decision on how it is distributed (the tool lives outside any plugin directory), and a check against a live gate agent in auto mode before WP-602 builds on it.
27	- Hook behavior on Claude Code 2.1.292: `onFailure: "block"` needs 2.1.295, so a crashing hook does not block (the validator fails open by design).
28	
29	## Change record (shared/harness-authoring.md)
30

## What the work found

- **`claude plugin validate plugins/<id>` was a false pass** because the manifests sit at the plugin root. With the generated `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` it validates the manifest, and the repo-only keys (`id`, `consumes`, `produces`) stay in `plugin.json` where Claude Code ignores them.
- **Recorded gate verdicts nearly all conform to their schemas.** 33 of 45 conform; all 12 violations are `verdict_summary` over 300 characters (`VERIFY-3.md` section 5). A hook would have asked for one trim on about 27% of handbacks.
- **`muse` gates mostly emitted `verdict@3`-shaped output** (26 of 36; the other 9 of the 45 files are `scribe` gates) while `muse` documented `verdict@1`, and its prompt told the agent to set `verdict` to `"escalate"`, which no schema allows. WP-02 (done) moved `muse` to `verdict@3` and made escalation an `escalation_required` blocker, as in the other four gates; the validator now checks `muse` against `verdict@3` only.
- **A bug in the validator was found only by real data:** a schema property with a list of types (`["string", "null"]`). It is fixed and has a regression test.
- **The `requirement@1` schema describes `reasoning` as "chain-of-thought during capture".** It is immutable (ADR 004), agents reach it through a file read and not a prompt, so the lint carries a documented exception; a future `requirement@2` should use the "private scratchpad" wording.

## Open items from this work

- The README documents AGY installs through the community `agy-plugins-cli`. Fetched source snippets suggest that tool discovers plugins as top-level repository directories, which would not find plugins under `plugins/`. This is unverified; test an install in an isolated environment before changing the README (WP-622, WP-621).
- The installed plugins use `shared -> ../../shared` symlinks and the Claude marketplace installs from the `plugins/<id>` subdirectory (`git-subdir`). Whether the symlink resolves after install is untested (WP-621).
- The hook is a spike: it needs a plugin `hooks/hooks.json` registration, a decision on how it is distributed (the tool lives outside any plugin directory), and a check against a live gate agent in auto mode before WP-602 builds on it.
- Hook behavior on Claude Code 2.1.292: `onFailure: "block"` needs 2.1.295, so a crashing hook does not block (the validator fails open by design).

```text
Classification: Codex workflow (role-card resource), distribution (generated bundle), shared identity (Claude manifest generation, root marketplace)
Counterpart reviewed: plugins/*/plugin.json, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, harnesses/codex/agent-roles/README.md, shared/harness-authoring.md, docs/codex-marketplace-release-policy.md

Verification: just check; just claude-validate; python3 -m unittest discover -s tests; scripts under docs/evaluations/frontend-design/verification/scripts
```

The repo's contribution checklist asks for a plugin version bump, a plugin changelog entry and a matching marketplace entry when a plugin's behavior changes, and the version check compares all of them. These changes touch every plugin's packaged files (the Codex role README, a new Claude manifest), so a release would bump all ten plugins and the ecosystem version together. That is a release decision, so no version, changelog or tag was changed. Until then `just versions` passes because nothing it compares moved, and the generated Claude manifests copy whatever version `plugin.json` has.

| Finding | Action | Evidence |

| `changeset@2` capped the summary at 200 characters and the agent, skill and schema repeated one-clause and one-sentence limits, so a limit users will hit went into the unforwarded `reasoning` | New `changeset@3` (no cap, Markdown, `disposition` of new, update-existing or none) and `release-artifact@3`; `changeset@2` and `release-artifact@2` are untouched per ADR 004 | `tests/test_changeset_schema.py` |

**Finding: `shared/...` reference paths depend on the working directory.** In that run the agent reported it could not find `shared/references/delivery/changesets.md` and fell back to the schema-implied rules. The agent was started from a directory outside the plugin, and its `load_first` paths are relative to the plugin root, not to where the agent runs. This is separate from, and in addition to, the dangling-symlink install defect fixed in the marketplace sources (VERIFY-3 section 7): even a correct install leaves a relative `shared/...` path unresolvable from a user's project. It likely explains the pilots where schema files were not readable at run time. Not fixed here. Options: pass the plugin root into the skill and agent instructions if the host substitutes it, name the references in the skill body so they load with it, or inline the few rules an agent cannot work without. Needs a host check first.

`pr-narrator` and `commit-analyzer` were then changed to match: they follow the repository's own conventions (a pull request template, recent commit scopes and subject style), keep limits in the body instead of the scratchpad, mark breaking changes to command output, exit codes and file formats, and the narrator names or recommends a changeset. Both agents again could not find their `shared/` reference, the working-directory finding above.

Not done: changes in the Callisto repo (its AGENTS.md or PR template), which are recommendations only: say in its AGENTS.md to invoke `courier/changeset` for changesets and `courier/pr` for PR text, and add a changeset prompt to its PR template.

ADR 014 supersedes ADR 009's every-task code requirement only | `tests/test_navigator_plan.py`; `just check` |

Measured once each (Sonnet 5.5, a two-task, six-criterion Python fixture with the schema path given in the prompt): the old planner wrote 9,777 characters (8 steps, 18 function definitions); the new one wrote 5,578 (18 steps, 1 definition). Not tested: whether implementers do better or worse from the smaller plans, and the challenger on either shape.

**Finding: without the schema in reach, the planner invents fields.** A first pair of runs started from a directory with no `shared/schemas` and both wrote task keys the schema forbids (`outcome`, `approach`, `tests`, `verify_command`), the same working-directory problem as the courier finding above. | The gate retry rule needs `retry_count` and the prior blockers as input; no skill passed them | One sentence in the gate-calling skills (muse `component`, scribe `gate-spec`, sentinel `gate`, smith `implement`, ranger `audit`) and the Codex counterparts | `just check` |
| Tracks B to E (gate hygiene, measurement, skill routing, planner) ran in parallel worktrees and were merged here | Merged with log-only conflicts resolved by keeping both sides | `just check` exit 0 after each merge |
| Nine plugins had changed against `main` with no version or changelog | muse 1.1.0, smith 2.5.0, navigator 2.4.0, scribe 3.5.0, courier 3.1.0; sentinel, ranger, mason, vanguard and weaver patch bumps; ecosystem 4.5.0 | `just versions`, `just check`, `just claude-validate` |

Limits: the path finding rests on single probe runs; Antigravity's handling of `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in skill and agent text was not tested, and its format shares the authored tree, so confirm it before releasing. The hook-only plugins (sentinel, ranger) are patch bumps although a gate can now deny a report that used to pass; scribe is a minor because its drafter and skills also changed behavior.

## Top-tier models removed

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Two agents (`scribe:arch-auditor`, `scribe:architect`) ran on `claude-fable-5-1`, about twice Opus, and `arch-auditor` runs on every spec; the Codex `judge` role ran on `gpt-6-astra`. The constitution said fable was never for gates or per-finding loops, and no measurement shows either tier catches more | Both scribe agents move to `opus / high`, the constitution drops the fable tier, the Codex `judge` moves to `gpt-6.1-sol / high`; tier tests updated | `just check`. Quality effect unmeasured: run the spec-gating paired comparison in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md` and restore a tier if boundary conflicts or binding verdicts are missed |

Codex `author` role: moved from `gpt-6.1-sol` / high to `gpt-6.1-terra` / medium (Terra is about half of Sol's price per token and is positioned for clear writing; the page lists no effort levels for it, so the effort label stays relative). Other roles unchanged. Unmeasured: whether Terra drafts specs, PR text and changesets as well as Sol; run the spec-drafting and courier comparisons in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md`.

## Model and effort fit

Audit of all 45 agents against the constitution's tiers (haiku/low for mechanical work, sonnet/medium for analysis and execution, opus/high for binding judgment). Two clear mismatches changed: `courier:release-summarizer` sonnet/medium to haiku/low (deterministic aggregation), `scribe:drift-checker` opus/high to sonnet/medium (a diagnostic, not a gate). Left alone pending measurement, in order of likely saving: `ranger:adversary` (one opus call per candidate), `scribe:arch-auditor` (opus on every spec), `sentinel:exit-gate` (maps a verifier report to a verdict without re-reading evidence, so it may not need opus), and whether opus gates need `high` rather than the default effort. Gate quality decides retry rounds, so a cheaper gate that misses more can cost more than it saves; test with the spec-gating comparison in `docs/evaluation-runbook.md` before changing them.

## Evidence review and ADR 015

Three independent reads (documented evidence; session token data over 1,555 subagent calls and 253M reported tokens in five projects; reviewer catch rate over about 400 runs) agreed the structure is partly worth it. Value came from first-round independent checks against code or a build; repeated rounds, the auditor and gate reviewing the same draft, per-commit review and mutation on type-only modules were waste; no reviewer caught a logic bug (28% of human-found findings); 77% of subagent tokens went to ad hoc general-purpose agents and forks, not plugins; plugin agents mostly ran without their skills. The second half of the catch-rate report was reconstructed from the agent's notes, so its exact counts are approximate.

Changed (ADR 015): two rounds for every exit gate and the challenger, escalation on a repeated blocker, hook cap `retry_count` above 1; drafter self-check then gate, with auditor, verifier and architecture audit on request or for shared or cross-module specs; spec gates check claims against their sources; review once per batch; mutation skipped when no executable logic changed. Versions: muse 1.2.0, scribe 3.6.0, smith 2.6.0, navigator 2.5.0, sentinel 2.1.4, ranger 3.2.5, ecosystem 4.6.0.

Next: behavior checks for the logic-bug gap; skills as the entry point (routing); collapsing build-side chains; main-loop cost (forks); measure with paired fix-task sequences.

Behavior checks and routing (same branch): `shared/references/verification/evidence.md` now says structure is not behavior (run changed logic on representative and edge inputs from the criterion or defect; inspect the built page for visual changes), and the smith reviewer and exit gate, ranger exit gate and sentinel verifier load it. 26 pipeline agents' descriptions now name the skill that starts them; resident agent description text fell from about 3,079 to 2,239 tokens. One live run (Sonnet 5.5, smith plugin, a two-line bug "add(2, 3) returns 6") used no skill or agent: the model fixed it directly and added a test that fails on the original bug. That run does not test routing, because direct work is proportionate for a bug that size; routing needs a multi-file task, measured with the runbook.

## Routing: entry commands and the routing guard

| Finding | Action | Evidence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Sessions called pipeline agents directly (318 agent calls against 12 skill uses in one Callisto session), so skill-level checks never ran; 33 skills named by plugin are hard to pick | New `guide` plugin: `/guide:explore`, `spike`, `fix`, `build`, `check`, `ship` hand off to the existing skills by risk; an `AGENTS.md` snippet in its README | `just check` |
| A prompt cannot force routing; a hook can see it. Traced on Claude Code with a probe plugin: a typed `/plugin:skill` arrives only as a `UserPromptSubmit` prompt, a model-started skill as a `PreToolUse` `Skill` call, a subagent call as a `PreToolUse` `Agent` call with `subagent_type`, all with one `session_id` | `shared/hooks/route-guard.py <plugin>`, registered by muse, navigator, ranger, scribe, sentinel and smith for their own agents: a direct call is denied once per agent per session until one of the plugin's skills has started, then goes through; fails open; `WISP_ROUTE_GUARD=off` disables it | `tests/test_route_guard.py` (6 tests); live run: "have smith:reviewer review calc.py" was denied once with the redirect and the explicit retry went through |

Limit, observed live: with `guide` and `smith` loaded, a generic "review my fix before I merge" was handled by the model itself (read, run tests) with no skill or agent, so the guard never fired. The guard stops agents being used without their checks; it does not make the model choose a skill. For that, the levers are the project's `AGENTS.md` (snippet in `plugins/guide/README.md`), typing the `/guide:` commands, and, if measurement shows substantive work still skipping checks, an outcome guard on code changes (not built).

# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.

- **`muse/sketch`** produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and a reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
- **`smith/spike`** produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works, with what was verified and what was not.
- **`muse/promote`** turns a chosen option or a working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
- Exploration modes are **non-binding**: no gate, no spec, no test requirement, open questions allowed. They write only to a scratch directory and to the artifact, mark it `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, and stop before implementing. An exploration artifact is never evidence for a gate.
- Divergent generation, producing structurally different options without judging them, is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`), as ADR 003 requires. Judging the options stays with the user.
- The modes and their rules live in one reference (`shared/references/architecture/modes.md`), loaded by the three skills. The skill is the entry point; its agents are internal.

## Why

The gated path (recon, a spec with no TBD, a binding exit gate, a plan, a challenger, implementation with mutation and review) earns its cost on a stable contract that other work depends on. It does not fit an idea nobody has seen yet. In the audited projects the specs described behavior well and appearance not at all, every spec failed its first gate, and the owner asked for drawings and rewrote the gated specs after seeing them. Design ideation then ran outside the plugins, in forks and general-purpose agents, at a token cost larger than all the gates together, and its decisions were lost between sessions. The plugin skills were almost never invoked, so agents reachable only through skills never ran. Industry practice points the same way: Vercel's product-design skill routes between a read-only shaping mode and a hardening mode, and Anthropic's guidance says exploratory work may skip planning.

## Rejected

- **Loosen the existing gates.** Gates earn their cost on stable contracts, and loosening them for everyone weakens the cases that need them.
- **A light flag on each existing skill.** One skill would carry two contracts, and orchestrators skip skills they find heavy; a separate, named, light skill is easier to choose and to evaluate.
- **A new plugin for exploration.** Deferred. `muse` is the only plugin that owns UI and design, and `AGENTS.md` lets one plugin hold several skills for heterogeneous intents. The artifact schema is UI-neutral so sketching can move into its own plugin if it is used outside UI work.
- **Leave exploration ad hoc.** It produced the largest token cost, the lost decisions and the unreviewed visual defects.

## Consequences

There is a named, light path for early work and a stated way back into the gated pipeline. The risks are that an exploration artifact is mistaken for a spec, and that the light path is used where the gated path is needed. The `fidelity` marker, the promote-only rule, the list of cases that must use the full pipeline in `modes.md`, and the required note of which gates were skipped address them. Each new skill and agent needs its Codex counterpart, and the new schemas are immutable once published (ADR 004).

Revisit when the evaluation in `docs/evaluation-methodology.md` shows the light path is chosen where the gated path is needed, or that it does not speed exploration without raising later defects.

**Evidence:** `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, section "ADR evidence", ADR 011.

# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

Ship one stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, and register it in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) through `hooks/hooks.json`.

- It acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table and lets every other subagent through.
- It validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules.
- It denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth report passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- It enforces the retry cap in the report: a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with a blocker whose criterion is `escalation_required`.
- It fails open: an internal error never blocks a subagent.
- `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` appends one line per inspected report, for evaluation.

The prompts keep stating the rules, so harnesses without the hook still get the instruction. The hook is the enforcement where the host supports it.

## Why

The schema and the retry cap lived only in prompts, and the audited runs broke both: gate verdicts violated the schema, specs passed their gate past the retry cap, and the `muse` gate was told to emit a verdict value no schema allows. A rule that matters in every run and can be checked by a program should not depend on a model remembering it. Claude Code delivers a subagent's report in auto mode through the `SubagentHandback` tool; a `PreToolUse` hook on it sees the report in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so the subagent corrects its output in place. The platform checks are in `docs/verified-facts.md`.

## Rejected

- **Keep the rules in prompts.** The recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill.** The orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct its own output in place.
- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop.** Deferred to WP-603; it can replace the cap check later, but the schema check is useful either way.
- **A third-party JSON Schema library.** Hooks run on user machines with no install step. The validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, and a test covers each.

## Consequences

Gate conformance is checked on every run in Claude Code auto mode, and the retry cap cannot be passed silently. Limits: the hook covers only the Claude Code host, only auto mode and only local, non-fork subagents. A hook failure or timeout does not block, because `onFailure: "block"` needs Claude Code 2.1.295. Plugin hooks fire for every subagent, so the routing table is the scope. Codex and Antigravity have no equivalent. A new gate agent needs a routing entry, and a schema that adds keywords needs the validator extended in the same change.

Revisit when `onFailure: "block"` is available on every supported host (fail closed instead of open), or when Codex or Antigravity gain an equivalent hook.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (the validator, and that every exit-gate agent is routed and its plugin registers the hook).

**Evidence:** `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, section "ADR evidence", ADR 012.

# ADR-013: Exit gates list the complete blocker set in round one and cite only known blockers on a retry

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10

## Decision

- Each exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) states two rules in its `<output>` section, worded the same in all five. In round one (`retry_count` 0 or absent) it lists the complete blocker set. On a retry it cites only blockers from the prior round that remain unresolved, or regressions the fix introduced; any other newly noticed issue is a `coverage_gaps` entry with `blocking: false`.
- A blocker names the criterion or section in `criterion`, cites evidence (quoted text or a location) in `finding`, and states the exact change required. A wording-only or style-only issue is a note, never a blocker.
- The drafters that feed a spec gate (`muse:drafter`, `scribe:drafter`) load `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` and check their draft against its spec checklist before returning. The checklist and blocker wording live in that one reference.
- `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py` additionally denies a blocker or coverage gap whose text field is only whitespace. It checks nothing else about blocker content.

Gates stay default-fail and adversarial; no pass condition is relaxed. `verdict@3` is unchanged.

## Why

Every audited spec failed its first gate, and blocker counts did not fall from round to round. A zero followed by a nonzero count means a later round found issues an earlier round could have found, or a fix broke something. Each extra round re-reads the whole artifact, so late-found issues are the expensive ones. ADR 012 enforces schema conformance and the retry cap by hook but not round discipline, and a program cannot judge round discipline, so it has to be a prompt rule on the gate plus a self-check on the drafter.

## Rejected

- **A `verdict@4` with a `regression` or `prior_blocker_id` field on each blocker.** `verdict@3` already expresses the rule through `blockers` and `coverage_gaps`, and ADR 004 makes a new schema version costly. Today the hook cannot tell fix-induced blockers from late-found ones anyway, because a retry is a new subagent with no stored prior verdict.
- **Hook checks that a blocker has a `location`, a minimum length, or a quote.** An `escalation_required` or `missing_mutation_gate` blocker has no location, and a terse correct blocker would be denied. Each denial costs a turn, so only blank text is rejected.
- **Make the gate lenient on retries (accept anything not previously listed).** The rule does not drop findings; it records them as non-blocking gaps the orchestrator sees.
- **Put the rule in the shared constitution.** The constitution is copied byte for byte into every agent (ADR 006), so a change touches all of them; the rule applies only to gates.

## Consequences

Fewer rounds and fewer tokens per gated spec, with the same defects caught; that is expected, not measured. Costs: a defect a gate misses in round one can now pass as a non-blocking gap on a retry, so the gap list needs a reader; and a gate can tell a retry from round one only if the orchestrator supplies `retry_count` and the prior blockers, so the gate-calling skills must carry them into the retry input.

Revisit when paired runs show round counts do not fall, or when the hook must tell fix-induced blockers from late-found ones (the `verdict@4` case).

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (blank text), `tests/test_agent_structure.py` and `tests/test_prompt_alignment.py` (agent shape). The round rules themselves are prompt rules.

**Evidence:** `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, section "ADR evidence", ADR 013.

# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10
**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.

## Decision

`planner` writes each task as an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`. It adds implementation code only where the logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape would be costly to undo: ordering or concurrency rules, numeric or parsing edge cases, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, algorithms the spec states only by result, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.

`challenger` flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified`, and treats a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`. It no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its checks for missing work, ordering, criterion coverage and sibling interfaces are unchanged.

No schema change. `plan@1` stays as published (ADR 004). The shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer that reads a plan (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already handles free-text steps.

ADR-009 stays Accepted as to implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; only its requirement that every task carry the exact code is superseded. Its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.

## Why

ADR-009 made the plan's code a baseline the implementer may reshape, but still required it for every task. So `planner` wrote a body for every function, `challenger` policed it, and `implementer` was told not to copy it. Three forces argue against that. Very large plans stalled agents in the audited projects. Anthropic's guidance says instructions written for earlier models are often too prescriptive for current ones and reduce output quality. And a body the implementer may discard buys little: the guardrail ADR-009 wanted is the plan's scope (files, signatures, tests, criteria), which does not need the body.

`plan@1` does not require code. A task requires `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` (an array of strings) and `commit_message`; "exact code" appears only in a field description, and `additionalProperties` is false, so everything else a task carries lives in `steps` strings.

## Rejected

- **Keep exact code for every task.** It is the cost this record exists to cut, and ADR-009 already made the code non-binding.
- **Drop code entirely.** A wrong shape in a wire format, a parsing edge or a cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent, and weaker implementers lose a guardrail.
- **A plan mode (outcome-level or full-code) chosen per run.** It doubles the planner and challenger surface to test, and a per-task rule covers both ends.
- **A `plan@2` with explicit outcome, signature and test fields.** The `steps` array carries the content, and a new version would need every consumer and the pipeline fixtures to move.
- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code.** A published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004); the descriptions are stale but harmless.

## Consequences

Plans are smaller. The risks are that an implementer on a weaker model invents a wrong shape where the plan gave only a signature, that a plan with no code is harder for `challenger` to falsify, and that the rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call the planner can get wrong in either direction.

Revisit when consumers need to read outcome, signature or test fields programmatically (a `plan@2`), or when implementers do measurably worse from outcome-level plans.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_navigator_plan.py` checks the planner and challenger rules, the unchanged schema, and that a plan in the new shape validates against `plan@1`.

**Evidence:** `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, sections "Outcome-level plans" and "ADR evidence", ADR 014.

`plan@1` does not require code. A task requires `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` (an array of strings) and `commit_message`; "exact code" appears only in a field description, and `additionalProperties` is false, so everything else a task carries lives in `steps` strings.

## Rejected

- **Keep exact code for every task.** It is the cost this record exists to cut, and ADR-009 already made the code non-binding.
- **Drop code entirely.** A wrong shape in a wire format, a parsing edge or a cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent, and weaker implementers lose a guardrail.
- **A plan mode (outcome-level or full-code) chosen per run.** It doubles the planner and challenger surface to test, and a per-task rule covers both ends.
- **A `plan@2` with explicit outcome, signature and test fields.** The `steps` array carries the content, and a new version would need every consumer and the pipeline fixtures to move.
- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code.** A published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004); the descriptions are stale but harmless.

## Consequences

Plans are smaller. The risks are that an implementer on a weaker model invents a wrong shape where the plan gave only a signature, that a plan with no code is harder for `challenger` to falsify, and that the rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call the planner can get wrong in either direction.

Revisit when consumers need to read outcome, signature or test fields programmatically (a `plan@2`), or when implementers do measurably worse from outcome-level plans.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_navigator_plan.py` checks the planner and challenger rules, the unchanged schema, and that a plan in the new shape validates against `plan@1`.

# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.

- **`muse/sketch`** produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and a reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
- **`smith/spike`** produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment that checks whether a tool or approach works, with what was verified and what was not.
- **`muse/promote`** turns a chosen option or a working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
- Exploration modes are **non-binding**: no gate, no spec, no test requirement, open questions allowed. They write only to a scratch directory and to the artifact, mark it `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, and stop before implementing. An exploration artifact is never evidence for a gate.
- Divergent generation, producing structurally different options without judging them, is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`), as ADR 003 requires. Judging the options stays with the user.
- The modes and their rules live in one reference (`shared/references/architecture/modes.md`), loaded by the three skills. The skill is the entry point; its agents are internal.

## Why

The gated path (recon, a spec with no TBD, a binding exit gate, a plan, a challenger, implementation with mutation and review) earns its cost on a stable contract that other work depends on. It does not fit an idea nobody has seen yet. In the audited projects the specs described behavior well and appearance not at all, every spec failed its first gate, and the owner asked for drawings and rewrote the gated specs after seeing them. Design ideation then ran outside the plugins, in forks and general-purpose agents, at a token cost larger than all the gates together, and its decisions were lost between sessions. The plugin skills were almost never invoked, so agents reachable only through skills never ran. Industry practice points the same way: Vercel's product-design skill routes between a read-only shaping mode and a hardening mode, and Anthropic's guidance says exploratory work may skip planning.

## Rejected

- **Loosen the existing gates.** Gates earn their cost on stable contracts, and loosening them for everyone weakens the cases that need them.
- **A light flag on each existing skill.** One skill would carry two contracts, and orchestrators skip skills they find heavy; a separate, named, light skill is easier to choose and to evaluate.
- **A new plugin for exploration.** Deferred. `muse` is the only plugin that owns UI and design, and `AGENTS.md` lets one plugin hold several skills for heterogeneous intents. The artifact schema is UI-neutral so sketching can move into its own plugin if it is used outside UI work.
- **Leave exploration ad hoc.** It produced the largest token cost, the lost decisions and the unreviewed visual defects.

## Consequences

There is a named, light path for early work and a stated way back into the gated pipeline. The risks are that an exploration artifact is mistaken for a spec, and that the light path is used where the gated path is needed. The `fidelity` marker, the promote-only rule, the list of cases that must use the full pipeline in `modes.md`, and the required note of which gates were skipped address them. Each new skill and agent needs its Codex counterpart, and the new schemas are immutable once published (ADR 004).

Revisit when the evaluation in `docs/evaluation-methodology.md` shows the light path is chosen where the gated path is needed, or that it does not speed exploration without raising later defects.

# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

Ship one stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, and register it in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) through `hooks/hooks.json`.

- It acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table and lets every other subagent through.
- It validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules.
- It denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth report passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- It enforces the retry cap in the report: a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with a blocker whose criterion is `escalation_required`.
- It fails open: an internal error never blocks a subagent.
- `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` appends one line per inspected report, for evaluation.

The prompts keep stating the rules, so harnesses without the hook still get the instruction. The hook is the enforcement where the host supports it.

## Why

The schema and the retry cap lived only in prompts, and the audited runs broke both: gate verdicts violated the schema, specs passed their gate past the retry cap, and the `muse` gate was told to emit a verdict value no schema allows. A rule that matters in every run and can be checked by a program should not depend on a model remembering it. Claude Code delivers a subagent's report in auto mode through the `SubagentHandback` tool; a `PreToolUse` hook on it sees the report in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so the subagent corrects its output in place. The platform checks are in `docs/verified-facts.md`.

## Rejected

- **Keep the rules in prompts.** The recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill.** The orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct its own output in place.
- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop.** Deferred to WP-603; it can replace the cap check later, but the schema check is useful either way.
- **A third-party JSON Schema library.** Hooks run on user machines with no install step. The validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, and a test covers each.

## Consequences

Gate conformance is checked on every run in Claude Code auto mode, and the retry cap cannot be passed silently. Limits: the hook covers only the Claude Code host, only auto mode and only local, non-fork subagents. A hook failure or timeout does not block, because `onFailure: "block"` needs Claude Code 2.1.295. Plugin hooks fire for every subagent, so the routing table is the scope. Codex and Antigravity have no equivalent. A new gate agent needs a routing entry, and a schema that adds keywords needs the validator extended in the same change.

Revisit when `onFailure: "block"` is available on every supported host (fail closed instead of open), or when Codex or Antigravity gain an equivalent hook.

**Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (the validator, and that every exit-gate agent is routed and its plugin registers the hook).

**Evidence:** `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, section "ADR evidence", ADR 012.
